passage_text: Researchers at the University of Health Sciences conducted a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial to evaluate the efficacy of the novel antihypertensive agent, Hypotensol, in adults with stage 1 hypertension. Eighty participants aged 35–65 were enrolled and randomly assigned to receive either 10 mg of Hypotensol once daily or a matching placebo for 12 weeks. Baseline systolic (SBP) and diastolic blood pressure (DBP) readings were obtained using an automated cuff after a 5‑minute rest period. At the end of the study, mean SBP and DBP values were compared between groups. Table 1 summarizes the key findings. In addition, researchers recorded adverse events, heart rate, and serum creatinine to assess safety. The investigators hypothesized that Hypotensol would lower SBP by at least 10 mmHg more than placebo, with a corresponding reduction in DBP. The trial was registered under ClinicalTrials.gov identifier NCT12345678. Results indicated a mean SBP reduction of 12.5 mmHg in the treatment group versus 3.2 mmHg in the placebo group, yielding a between‑group difference of 9.3 mmHg (95% CI 6.1–12.5). DBP decreased by 7.8 mmHg in the treatment arm compared to 1.5 mmHg in controls. The drug was well tolerated, with mild headaches reported in 5% of participants.
stem: What was the mean systolic blood pressure reduction observed in the Hypotensol treatment group?
explanation: The study reports a mean SBP reduction of 12.5 mmHg in the Hypotensol group.
trap: Reporting the between-group difference (9.3 mmHg) or the DBP reduction (7.8 mmHg) instead of the treatment group's SBP reduction.

stem: Which feature of the trial best protects against participants' and investigators' expectations influencing the measured SBP and reported effects?

options.A: Double-blind administration with a matching placebo
options.B: Use of an automated cuff after 5 minutes' rest only
options.C: Registration of the trial on ClinicalTrials.gov
options.D: Recording adverse events and serum creatinine

explanation: Correct: Double-blinding with a matching placebo keeps both participants and investigators unaware of assignment, limiting performance and detection bias. Why the others are wrong: B) A standardized cuff reduces measurement variability but does not hide treatment assignment. C) Registration promotes transparency about planned outcomes; it does not blind anyone. D) Safety recording assesses tolerability, not bias in efficacy assessment.
trap: Picking randomization or standardized measurement, which do not conceal assignment.

stem: The investigators hypothesized a between-group SBP difference of at least 10 mmHg. Which statement correctly compares the results with that target?

options.A: The observed difference was 9.3 mmHg, slightly below 10, and its 95% CI (6.1–12.5) includes 10 mmHg, so the target was neither clearly met nor clearly missed
options.C: The observed difference was 12.5 mmHg, which exceeds the target
options.D: The 95% CI for the difference lies entirely below 10 mmHg

explanation: Correct: The between-group difference was 12.5 − 3.2 = 9.3 mmHg, below 10, but the 95% CI of 6.1 to 12.5 mmHg includes 10, so the data are compatible with a true difference on either side of the target. Why the others are wrong: B) 9.3 mmHg is less than 10 mmHg. C) 12.5 mmHg is the treatment group's own reduction, not the difference from placebo. D) the upper confidence limit, 12.5 mmHg, is above 10 mmHg.
trap: Comparing the treatment group's own reduction (12.5) with a target that refers to the difference from placebo.
